AUGHRIM VISITOR CENTRE – SUMMER SERIES 2025 
  
The Aughrim Visitor Centre has successfully 
delivered three of its' five scheduled events 
for its' Summer Series 2025.   
Each event has celebrated a unique aspect 
of Irish heritage, creativity, and historical 
reflection. The series has proven to be a 
vibrant platform for community 
engagement, education, and cultural 
enrichment.  
 
Launched on June 20th with “A Rich Harvest of Irish Musical Creativity & Composition”, our 
inaugural 2025 event, drew a huge turnout with wonderful community support. 
  
Attendees enjoyed a lively presentation 
celebrating Ireland’s musical legacy, with 
particular emphasis on composition and 
creativity. The event set a high standard for 
the series and highlighted the Centre’s role in 
promoting cultural dialogue.

GOOD NEWS STORY: BALLINASLOE AND TUAM LEISURE CENTRES -   
ENHANCEMENT  
Ballinasloe and Tuam Leisure Centres have been recently enhanced through a refurbishment 
of their changing room facilities, thanks to funding secured by Galway County Council 
through Sports Capital Grants.  
These investments will improve the hygiene, functionality, and overall user experience of 
the centres, addressing long-standing concerns raised by both Leisure Centres' staff and 
members, as these centres approach their 20th year in operation.  
The Facilities team within Corporate Services played a pivotal role in delivering this project.  
From the initial tendering process to researching the most suitable best practice flooring 
materials available, coordinating contractor engagement, and supervising the works on-site, 
these projects have been executed to a very high standard and within scope.  
The teams' hands-on involvement was critical in achieving upgrades that meet both 
operational and user needs. 
Scope of Works Completed at each Leisure Centre: 
• Removal and storage of existing cubicles for reuse. 
• Demolition of six internal walls in male and female changing rooms. 
• Removal of outdated shower units and skirting tiles. 
• Preparation of floors for new resin flooring, chosen for its durability and ease of 
cleaning. 
• Installation of whiterock sheeting in shower areas to improve hygiene and 
aesthetics. 
• Application of resin flooring in changing rooms and poolside showers. 
• Installation of new, modern shower units. 
• Retiling around showers adjacent to the steam room. 
• Reinstallation and fitting of new cubicles. 
• Final cleaning and preparation for reopening. 
These refurbishments are not just cosmetic—they directly address key issues identified 
during staff consultations in both leisure centres. The previous flooring and wall tiles had 
become “impossible to keep clean,” negatively impacting membership renewals and new 
sign-ups. 
The new resin floors and whiterock wall cladding now offer a brighter, cleaner, and more 
hygienic environment, making daily cleaning faster and more effective."

At this event 29 PAW heroes from across Galway City and Galway County who exemplify

TOWN AND VILLAGE RENEWAL, GORT STREETSCAPE SCHEME  
Gort Town Team have continued to work with the County Council Rural Development Team 
to encourage the completion of shopfront repair and painting upgrades to the Main Square, 
Crowe and Bridge Steet in Gort. Significant progress has been made during July and August 
2025 with a strong visual impact evident in the Town Centre and over €67,000 has been 
paid to Property Owners and Leaseholders to date under the Scheme.  
A total of 70 properties have been offered grant aid in the period since November 2024 
where detailed Offers were issued on the foot of a Scheme Launch in June 2024.  
On March 6th 2025, a ‘Spring into Action’ Scheme Re-launch Event was held in Gort Town 
Hall. The session provided invaluable insights, on conservation, best practice and how to 
finalise colour consultants and funding claims with presentation by Galway County Council 
Conservation Officer (Ann Marie Cusask) on the Gort ACA (Architectural Conservation Area). 
Carpenters, Painters and Local Sign-Writers were also in attendance to provide advise to 
approved applicants.  Administrative Staff from the Rural Development Team in the 
Community Section of the Council staff held information clinics at the Gort Resource Centre 
to assist property owners to file their funding claims on the 14/5/2025, 24/6/2025 and again 
at the end of July 31/7/2025. A further ‘clinic’ session will be held in September.

GALWAY CITY OF FILM/ CEANTAR SCANNÁN 
Congratulations to Oisín and Saidbh Mac Coille who have received our Ceantar Scannán 
Short Documentary Bursary 2025. 
Oisín Mac Coille is a Galway-based writer and director with a background in short film and 
television. Originally from Cork, he has been living and working in Galway for almost twenty 
years.

26 
 
Oisín’s work focuses on telling personal, human stories with honesty, care, and an eye for 
the quiet moments that often go unnoticed. His project, ‘Art That Rises’, follows his ten-
year-old daughter, Saidbh, as she searches for belonging and joy after being diagnosed with 
Type 1 diabetes at the age of eight.   
Like many children living with lifelong conditions, Saidbh has faced challenges that have left 
her feeling isolated or different. The film captures the simple but powerful moments where 
creativity offers her — and others — the chance to belong, to feel normal, and to just be a 
child again.   
Oisín’s work is shaped by real-life experiences, with a focus on quiet resilience, small joys, 
and the stories often happening just beneath the surface. When not working, he’s usually 
found being kept busy by his daughters or figuring out the next story worth telling. 
The Short Documentary Bursary is managed on our behalf by Ardán. Oisín and Saidbh will 
receive €3,000 to help them make a short 
documentary of between five and fifteen 
minutes in duration. Alongside the bursary, 
they will be mentored by filmmaker Donal 
Haughey.

BOOK RETURNED AFTER 100 YEARS, BORROWED FROM THE CARNEGIE LIBRARY 
 
This book which has recently been returned to Galway 
Public Libraries, was originally borrowed around 100 years 
ago, between the years of 1924-1926. Galway County 
Council took over the running of the County Library 
service in 1926. Before this, from 1924-1926, the Library 
Service was operated by the Carnegie Trust, under the 
Carnegie Rural Libraries’ Scheme. The book is a 1923 
edition of Rudyard Kipling’s, "Plain tales from the Hills". It 
has a Carnegie Trust Label, but no stamp or label of 
Galway County Libraries, which were placed on all books 
after 1926. This means that this book was borrowed 
between 1924-1926 from the Carnegie Trust Rural 
Libraries Scheme, and it is fitting that it has now been returned, after 100 years on loan, 
having been discovered during a house clearance in Loughrea. Other than small wear and tear 
and yellowing pages, this 102 year old book is in very good condition, and it even contains a 
cutting from an old newspaper, a picture of a lady in a cart driven by a Shetland pony, which 
has been dated to the Irish Independent of 
September 27th, 1930, and obviously placed in 
the book by the person who had borrowed it 
some years prior to 1930, and this date from the 
newspaper cutting confirms the general timeline 
in which the book was borrowed. The book will be 
added to our special collections, as it is now of 
historic interest

RESTORATION IMPROVEMENT (RI) AND RESTORATION MAINTENANCE (RM) 
In 2025, Galway County Council was grant funded by the Department of Transport to the 
value of €22.65m for RI projects, and €5.33m for RM projects. 
Each MD has provided individual progress updates, including photos of completed works, 
however, on a countywide basis the RI programme is now approximately 75% complete, 
with the RM 100% complete. 
The RI grant is aimed at strengthening the structural integrity of the road network. These 
works are essential for extending the lifespan of roads and ensuring they can handle current 
and future traffic volumes, and typically involves: 
• Overlaying existing road surfaces with new materials to improve durability. 
• Addressing structural deficiencies in the pavement, including drainage. 
• Enhancing the road to meet modern standards for safety and usability, including 
signage and road markings. 
  
The RM grant focuses on preserving the existing road surface through: 
• Surface dressing, which involves applying a bituminous binder followed by a layer of 
chippings. 
• Basic preparatory works such as patching and cleaning before dressing. 
The goal is to protect the road before it deteriorates to the point of needing full restoration 
– a cost-effective way to maintain road quality and safety.

EAST GALWAY SWIFT SURVEY 
As part of the implementation of Galway County Heritage and Biodiversity Plan 2024–2030, 
a public engagement event was held under the East Galway Swift Project, which is 
supported by Galway County Council and The Heritage Council. This National Heritage Week 
event focused on raising awareness about swift conservation and the role of local 
communities in protecting this iconic migratory species.

150 
 
 
 We were pleased to welcome Éabha Garry from BirdWatch Ireland, who presented findings 
from her summer survey work conducted across East Galway. Her talk provided valuable 
insights into swift nesting behaviour, population trends, and the challenges facing the 
species due to habitat loss and modern building practices. The presentation underscored 
the importance of targeted conservation actions, such as the installation of swift nest boxes 
and the protection of traditional nesting sites in older buildings. 
Swifts (Apus apus) are a red-listed species in Ireland, meaning they are of high conservation 
concern. Their numbers have declined significantly in recent decades, primarily due to the 
loss of nesting sites. These birds are summer visitors, arriving in Ireland in May and 
departing by late August. They are dependent on urban and village architecture for nesting, 
making community involvement essential to their conservation. The East Galway Swift 
Project aims to address these challenges through education, habitat enhancement, and 
collaboration with local stakeholders. 
The event was hosted in partnership with Loughrea Tidy Towns at Comworks and they 
supported the coordination of the evening. Their contribution was instrumental in ensuring

HEADFORD JUNCTION SAFETY IMPROVEMENTS 
 Significant progress has been made to improve safety for children accessing Headford 
National School, the local crèche, and Presentation College, Headford 
Numerous concerns have been raised regarding pedestrian safety at this junction, 
particularly during peak school hours. In response, a series of targeted measures have been 
introduced to improve conditions for vulnerable road users. 
The completed works under this scheme included: 
• A new pedestrian crossing 
• Widened footpaths 
• Full road overlay with updated road markings 
• An age-friendly parking space 
 
 
 
 
 
These improvements aim to create a safer, more accessible environment for all road users, 
particularly schoolchildren and older residents.
